questions.prompt: Explain the GIL. Given that, how do you write concurrent Python?
questions.zh: 解释一下 GIL。有了它，你会怎么写并发的 Python？
outline: The GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time
Threads still work well for I/O-bound work, because the GIL is released while waiting
CPU-bound work goes to a process pool to use several cores
asyncio fits when there are many connections and little computation
A free-threaded build exists now, but most deployments still have the GIL

questions.prompt: Tell me about the pitfalls of async Python. What do you watch out for?
questions.zh: 讲讲异步 Python 的坑。你会注意什么？
outline: One blocking call inside a coroutine freezes the whole event loop
CPU work or blocking I/O must be handed to an executor
Cancellation is cooperative: tasks need cleanup in finally blocks
Timeouts and exception groups make failures visible instead of silent
How I test it: load the endpoint and watch for loop stalls

questions.prompt: What Python gotchas would you warn a junior developer about?
questions.zh: 有哪些 Python 的坑你会提醒初级开发者？
outline: A mutable default argument is shared between calls
Shallow copy versus deep copy when mutating nested data
Mutating a list while iterating over it skips elements
Naive versus aware datetimes cause subtle timezone bugs
Most of these bite silently, so tests matter more than memorization

questions.prompt: How do you keep a Python project maintainable once it is in production?
questions.zh: 一个 Python 项目上了生产之后，你怎么保持它可维护？
outline: Type hints on public functions, checked by a static type checker in CI
A virtual environment per project and pinned dependencies
dataclasses or TypedDict at the boundaries instead of loose dicts
pytest fixtures and parametrized tests keep the suite small
One linter-formatter, ruff, so style stops being a discussion

questions.prompt: A Python job is too slow. Walk me through how you would speed it up.
questions.zh: 一个 Python 任务太慢了。带我过一遍你会怎么优化。
outline: Profile the code first; the slow part is rarely where you guess
Fix the algorithm or the data structure before micro-optimizing
Cache repeated work with lru_cache where the inputs repeat
Generators keep memory flat on large inputs
Still CPU-bound: a process pool, or a C extension for the hot loop

outline: A timing decorator wraps my script entry points for profiling
Context managers own files and connections so cleanup is automatic
A property decorator turned computed fields into clean attributes
One classmethod factory reads better than three constructors
I keep decorators thin; the dunder plumbing stays boring on purpose

A static type checker catches the rename I only half-finished
Duck typing still wins for small glue functions
TypedDict describes JSON payloads without a class zoo
Structural typing lets test doubles fit without inheritance

A generator turned the pipeline into one line at a time
The iterator protocol is what makes the chain composable
Reference counting freed each line as the pipeline advanced
Caching the hot lookup with lru_cache removed the next bottleneck

questions.zh: Python 的环境管理名声在外。讲讲你最惨的一次依赖之战，以及你现在信任的配置。

The dependency resolver had silently chosen incompatible versions
Now every project gets a virtual environment from day one
Dependencies are pinned and the pyproject file is the source of truth
An editable install keeps the tool hackable while it matures

questions.prompt: How do you cancel asyncio tasks cleanly in Python? What breaks if you just kill them?
questions.zh: 在 Python 里怎么干净地取消 asyncio 任务？直接杀掉会坏什么？
outline: Cancellation arrives as an exception at the next await point
Shielded cleanup must finish, or connections leak silently
An exception group surfaces several failures instead of hiding them
A blocking call inside a task stalls cancellation for everyone
I test cancellation like a feature, not an afterthought

questions.zh: 你怎么给一个个人用的 Python 工具写测试，又不把它变成第二份工作？
outline: I test behavior at the boundary, not internals that change weekly
A pytest fixture builds the same tiny workspace for every test
Parametrizing covers the input table that used to be copy-pasted
Mocks stop at the boundary: network and clock, nothing deeper
Coverage targets the code paths I would cry about breaking

questions.prompt: Threads, processes, or asyncio: how do you choose for a Python job in your own projects?
questions.zh: 线程、进程还是 asyncio：你自己的项目里怎么选？
outline: IO-bound work starts on asyncio or plain threads, whichever reads simpler
CPU-bound work goes to a process pool to escape the lock
The global interpreter lock is the fact every choice respects
concurrent.futures lets me pilot threads, then swap in processes
Free-threaded builds may rewrite this answer; I benchmark before believing

Worker processes scale the stateless parts horizontally

questions.prompt: Explain how Python reclaims memory, and tell me about hunting a leak in a long-running script.
questions.zh: 讲讲 Python 怎么回收内存，再讲一次你在长跑脚本里抓内存泄漏的经历。
outline: Reference counting frees most objects the moment counts drop to zero
Cycles survive counting, so a cyclic collector sweeps them later
My leak was a cache: strong references kept every result forever
A weak reference cache let entries die with their owners
Passed by object reference explains why the cache mutated shared state
